claim: Transfer learning is the re-application of previously learned higher-level regularities to novel input.
source: Transfer learning, the re-application of previously learned higher-level regularities to novel input, is a key challenge in cognition.
evidence: This is a definitional statement provided in the abstract that establishes the meaning of transfer learning for the study.

claim: Previous empirical studies on transfer learning focused on supervised or reinforcement learning domains and mainly dealt with explicit knowledge.
source: Previous empirical studies on transfer learning focused on the domains of supervised or reinforcement learning and mainly dealt with explicit knowledge.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature in the introduction section.

claim: A large part of ecologically relevant learning happens implicitly.
source: it ignores the fact that a large part of ecologically relevant learning happens implicitly (Reber, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reber, 1989.

claim: Much ecologically relevant learning occurs in the absence of supervision or reinforcement.
source: it ignores the fact that a large part of ecologically relevant learning happens implicitly (Reber, 1989) and in the absence of supervision or reinforcement (Hinton, 2014; Hinton, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hinton, 2014 and Hinton, 2010.

claim: It is unknown whether and how humans' transfer learning operates during unsupervised learning and in the absence of explicit knowledge.
source: It is, therefore, an open question whether and how humans' transfer learning operates during unsupervised learning and in the absence of explicit knowledge.
evidence: This is stated as a research gap that motivates the current study.

claim: Explicit and implicit forms of learning can show different outcomes and learning trajectories.
source: previous studies demonstrated that explicit and implicit forms of learning can show different outcomes and learning trajectories (Ball et al., 2021; Bloch et al., 2016; Dale et al., 2012; Forano et al., 2021; Mathews et al., 1989; Poh and Taylor, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The role of consolidation in structural abstraction and transfer has been demonstrated previously for explicit learning with supervision or feedback.
source: the role of consolidation in structural abstraction and transfer has been demonstrated previously for explicit learning with supervision or feedback (Chambers, 2017; Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Klinzing et al., 2019; Lerner and Gluck, 2019; Lewis and Durrant, 2011; Rasch and Born, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on consolidation.

claim: There exist interactions between the level of explicitness and consolidation.
source: since there exist interactions between the level of explicitness and consolidation (Fischer et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2023; Robertson et al., 2004; Wagner et al., 2004; Zander et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The study paradigm builds on the classical spatial visual statistical learning (SVSL) design.
source: Our paradigm builds on the classical spatial visual statistical learning (SVSL) design (Fiser and Aslin, 2001) and extends it to a transfer learning setup.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the study design with a citation to the original SVSL paradigm.

claim: The paradigm combines the challenge of segmentation based on co-occurrence statistics with the abstraction and reapplication of shared structures.
source: This paradigm, therefore, combines the challenge of segmentation based on co-occurrence statistics (statistical learning) with the abstraction and reapplication of shared structures (transfer learning)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm design.

claim: During unsupervised learning, the transfer of learned structures is immediately possible when explicit knowledge is acquired.
source: Our results show that during unsupervised learning, the transfer of learned structures is immediately possible when explicit knowledge is acquired.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: When only implicit knowledge is obtained, immediate transfer leads to an interference between old knowledge and new learning.
source: In contrast, when only implicit knowledge is obtained, immediate transfer leads to an opposite effect, an interference between old knowledge and new learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: After 12-hour sleep consolidation following the learning of the first structure, implicit observers showed the same pattern of transfer as explicit observers did.
source: However, after 12-hour sleep consolidation following the learning of the first structure, while the knowledge still remains implicit, the same successful transfer of learned structures (i.e., generalization) occurs as in the explicit condition.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: The effect of sleep consolidation on implicit transfer is specific to sleep and not found after non-sleep consolidation.
source: This effect was specific to sleep and not found after non-sleep consolidation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: Adult and infant humans, as well as various other species, automatically and implicitly extract the underlying pair structure of SVSL scenes.
source: Adult and infant humans, as well as various other species, have been shown to automatically and implicitly extract the underlying pair structure of such scenes (Fiser and Aslin, 2002; Lee et al., 2021; Santolin and Saffran, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on SVSL.

claim: In Experiment 1, explicit participants performed significantly better than implicit participants for Phase 1 pairs.
source: In addition, the explicit participants (n=34) performed significantly better than the implicit ones as shown by a Welch's t-test (n=192) (d=0.73, t(224)=2.75, p=0.009) (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Experiment 1, explicit participants performed above chance for learning pairs that shared their higher-level orientation structure with Phase 1 pairs.
source: For Phase 2 pairs, explicit participants performed above chance for learning pairs that shared their higher-level orientation structure with that of pairs in Phase 1 (M=67.6, SE=6.3, d=0.48, t(33)=2.81, p=0.033, BF=5.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, implicit participants performed significantly above chance for pairs of the novel structure but not for pairs sharing the higher-level orientation structure with Phase 1.
source: In contrast to the explicit participants, implicit participants showed the opposite pattern, performing significantly above chance for pairs of the novel structure (M=57.8, SE=1.9, d=0.30, t(191)=4.16, p<0.001, BF=281) but demonstrated strong evidence that they did not learn pairs sharing the higher-level orientation structure with pairs in Phase 1 (M=49.1, SE=2.1, d=0.03, t(191)=–0.44, p=0.659, BF=0.09).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant correlation between explicit participants' overall learning in Phase 1 and learning of pairs with the same structure in Phase 2.
source: There was a significant and medium-to-large size correlation between overall learning in the first training phase and learning of pairs with the same structure in the second training phase (r=0.45, p=0.008)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was no correlation between explicit participants' overall learning in Phase 1 and learning of pairs with novel structure in Phase 2.
source: while this correlation was absent between the same overall learning in the first learning phase and learning of pairs with novel structure in the second learning phase (r=−0.01, p=0.947).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a significant interaction between participant type (explicit/implicit) and structure type (same/novel) factors.
source: as indicated by the significant interaction between the two factors (participant type and structure type) of the two-factor mixed ANOVA results (F(1,224)=4.89, p=0.028, BF=31.6, ηp2=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, implicit learners performed above chance for pairs of the same structure but not for pairs of the novel structure in Phase 2.
source: Implicit learners (n=140) also performed above chance for pairs of the same structure (M=58.8, SE=2.5, d=0.30, t(139)=3.51, p=0.004, BF=37.6), but not for pairs of the novel structure (M=46.8, SE=2.6, d=0.11, t(139)=–1.24, p=0.435, BF=0.27).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the performance difference between same and novel structure pairs was significant for implicit learners.
source: The performance difference between these two types of pairs was significant (Mdiff=11.96, d=0.24, t(139)=2.82, p=0.027, BF=5.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, implicit learners performed at chance with both pairs of the same structure and pairs of a novel structure in Phase 2.
source: The results of the implicit learners (n=150) provided strong evidence against generalization as they performed at chance with both pairs of the same structure (M=51.8, SE=2.3, d=0.07, t(149)=0.80, p=0.999, BF=0.17) and pairs of a novel structure (M=52.8, SE=2.6, d=0.09, t(149)=1.08, p=0.999, BF=0.22) of Phase 2 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3 and reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Experiment 3, explicit participants performed above chance for pairs of the same structure but not for pairs of a novel structure.
source: In contrast, participants with explicit knowledge (n=20) replicated the results of Experiments 1 and 2, with percent correct above chance for pairs of the same structure (M=70.0, SE=6.2, d=0.72, t(19)=3.24, p=0.026, BF = 10.4) but not for pairs of a novel structure (M=62.5, SE=7.4, d=0.38, t(19)=1.70, p=0.530, BF=0.78).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Experiment 4 replicated the results of Experiment 2 for implicit learners, showing stronger learning for pairs of the same structure compared to pairs of the novel structure.
source: The results of Experiment 4 replicated the results of Experiment 2 for implicit learners, showing stronger learning for pairs of the same structure as compared to pairs of the novel structure (Mdiff=11.04, d=0.23, t(144)=2.75, p=0.021, BF=4.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The difference for implicit learners between sleep and non-sleep conditions was not based on a time-of-day effect.
source: We, therefore, conclude that the difference for implicit learners between our previous sleep and non-sleep conditions was not based on a time-of-day effect.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison of results from Experiments 2, 3, and 4.

claim: A 4 × 2 ANOVA on implicit participants from Experiments 1-4 showed a significant interaction between consolidation type and pair type with no significant main effects.
source: The obtained results showed the typical pattern of a cross-over interaction with no significant main effects (consolidation type: F(3,623)=0.18, p=0.910, BF=0.003, ηp2=0.0009; pair type: F(1,623)=1.52, p=0.218, BF=0.17, ηp2=0.002) but a significant interaction (F(3,623)=7.43, p<0.001, BF=1979, ηp2=0.03).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis combining data from Experiments 1-4.

claim: Post hoc tests revealed significant differences between the no-consolidation group and the two asleep-consolidation groups for implicit learners.
source: Post hoc tests also revealed significant differences between the no-consolidation group (Experiment 1) and the two asleep-consolidation groups (Experiments 2 and 4), where the no-consolidation group showed stronger learning of novel structure pairs (Experiment 1 vs. Experiment 2: p=0.004, BF=44.3; Experiment 1 vs. Experiment 4: p=0.012; BF=12.7), while the asleep-consolidation groups showed stronger learning of same structure pairs (Experiment 1 vs. Experiment 2: p=0.015, BF=8.8; Experiment 1 vs. Experiment 4: p=0.011; BF = 14.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by post hoc statistical analysis of data from Experiments 1, 2, and 4.

claim: Matched implicit participants showed the same overall pattern of generalization behavior as the full sample of implicit participants for all four experiments.
source: Matched implicit participants showed the same overall pattern of generalization behavior as the full sample of implicit participants for all four experiments (Figure 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by matched sample analysis and reference to Figure 3.

claim: The difference in structural transfer is based predominantly on the quality of knowledge (its explicitness) not the exact level of learning.
source: Therefore, we posit that these findings strongly support the notion that the difference in the structural transfer is based predominantly on the quality of knowledge – its explicitness – not the exact level of learning.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the matched sample analysis results.

claim: In Experiment 5, participants had above-chance performance for Phase 1 and for same structure pairs but not novel structure pairs in Phase 2.
source: The participants had an above-chance performance for Phase 1 (M=71.8, SE=3.6, d=1.01, t(35)=6.07, p<0.001, BF = 26,395) and for the same structure (M=72.9, SE=4.0, d=0.95, t(35)=5.69, p<0.001, BF=9058) but not novel structure pairs (M=52.8, SE=5.8, d=0.08, t(35)=0.48, p=0.634, BF=0.20) in Phase 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 5.

claim: In Experiment 5, the performance for pairs of the same and novel structure was significantly different.
source: The performance for pairs of the same and novel structure was significantly different (d=0.64, t(35)=3.83, p=0.001, BF=58.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 5.

claim: Generalization producing immediate transfer between contexts can be easily induced by verbal instructions.
source: These results confirm that the generalization producing an immediate transfer between contexts can be easily induced by verbal instructions in any population
evidence: This conclusion is based on the results of Experiment 5.

claim: Over all experiments, explicit participants showed overall higher performance on same structure pairs than novel structure pairs.
source: The results showed an overall higher performance on same structure pairs than novel structure pairs for explicit participants (d=0.34, t(233.99)=2.56, p=0.011, BF=3.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis combining data from Experiments 1-4 and Supplementary Experiment 1.

claim: Over all experiments, explicit participants' performance for Phase 1 only significantly correlated with learning of same structure pairs, not novel structure pairs.
source: Furthermore, over all experiments, explicit participants' performance for Phase 1 only significantly correlated with learning of same structure pairs (r=0.41, p<0.001, BF=4460), not novel structure pairs (r=0.14, p=0.137, BF=0.62).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis combining data from multiple experiments.

claim: Sleep consolidation leads to an internal redescription of acquired knowledge by factorization, representing orientation as a useful summary statistic.
source: Our interpretation of these results is that sleep consolidation leads to an internal redescription of the acquired knowledge by factorization, that is, by representing the feature of orientation as a useful summary statistic in its own right.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results proposed by the authors.

claim: Without redescription of knowledge, previously learned patterns in Phase 1 interfere with new ones in Phase 2.
source: Without such a redescription, the previously learned patterns in Phase 1 interfere with new ones in Phase 2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, specifically the structural novelty effect observed in implicit learners without consolidation.

claim: When redescription occurs, abstract knowledge at the higher level of the hierarchy can be generalized to new input.
source: When redescription occurs, the abstract knowledge at the higher level of the hierarchy can be generalized, that is, it can be used during the processing and segmentation of new input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, specifically the transfer effect observed after sleep consolidation.

claim: The study's approach to hierarchy is different from earlier treatments of statistical learning in hierarchical systems.
source: Thus, our approach to hierarchy is different from earlier treatments of SL in hierarchical systems that focused on hierarchies of composition (Lee et al., 2021) or hierarchies that arbitrated between competing learning systems (Maheu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work with citations.

claim: Previous studies on statistical learning demonstrated that it is biased by prior knowledge acquired over a lifetime or shorter period.
source: Previous studies demonstrated that statistical learning is not based solely on momentarily observable co-occurrence statistics but is also biased by prior knowledge. However, these studies demonstrate various effects of prior knowledge acquired over a lifetime (Stärk et al., 2023) or shorter period (Antovich and Graf Estes, 2023; Chough and Zinszer, 2022; Kóbor et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The current study investigated structure-related effects that could not be explained by the transfer of token-level knowledge.
source: In contrast, the current study investigated structure-related effects that could not be explained by the transfer of token-level knowledge, and it strictly controlled the amount of previous exposure to the target structure.
evidence: This is a description of the study's methodological approach.

claim: Chunks acquired during statistical learning are organized into higher-level categories based on common underlying structures.
source: Our results demonstrate that similar to objects (Ashby and Maddox, 2005; Richler and Palmeri, 2014), chunks acquired during SL are not represented simply as an unrelated set of inventory elements but organized into higher-level categories based on the common underlying structures – for example, the category of horizontal pairs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with comparison to prior work on object representation.

claim: The results build a bridge between classical statistical learning and category learning.
source: Thus, our results build a bridge between classical SL and category learning
evidence: This is an interpretation of the broader implications of the results.

claim: Statistical learning is a vehicle for acquiring object-like representations.
source: it supports the idea that SL is a vehicle for acquiring object-like representations.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to earlier findings (Lengyel et al., 2019; Lengyel et al., 2021).

claim: Previous studies on statistical learning and consolidation obtained mixed results regarding the effects of time or sleep.
source: Previous studies on statistical learning and consolidation focused on how much time or sleep helps with the stabilization or improvement of specific memory traces and obtained mixed results, with some studies showing clear effects (Durrant et al., 2013; Durrant et al., 2016; Hennies et al., 2014; Lewis and Durrant, 2011) and others showing no or very limited effects of sleep (Arciuli and Simpson, 2012; Hallgató et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2009; McDevitt et al., 2022; Nemeth et al., 2010; Quentin et al., 2021; Simor et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies showing different results.

claim: The current study shows no evidence of a direct effect of sleep on statistical learning per se.
source: Our results are in line with the latter set of studies, showing no evidence of a direct effect of sleep on statistical learning per se; that is, no effect on the learning of specific item-item associations.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The study used the ability to generalize structure between learning contexts as the primary measure.
source: In contrast, our study specifically focused on the difference between explicit and implicit learners to disentangle the complex nature of consolidation, and we used the ability to generalize structure between learning contexts as our primary measure.
evidence: This is a description of the study's methodological approach.

claim: There is a similarity between consolidation benefits based on abstraction and generalization in explicit and implicit learning domains.
source: This approach allowed us to compare our findings to those reported in the domain of explicit learning (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Lerner and Gluck, 2019; Lewis and Durrant, 2011; Stickgold and Walker, 2013), under names such as schemas (Lewis and Durrant, 2011), rules (Lerner and Gluck, 2019), insight (Wagner et al., 2004), and gist (Lutz et al., 2017), and uncover a surprising similarity between consolidation benefits based on abstraction and generalization in the two domains.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the current results to prior work in explicit learning.

claim: Implicit learners required sleep to 'uncover' abstract higher-level descriptors of observed structures and utilize them in subsequent implicit learning.
source: In particular, similarly to observers who needed sleep to 'discover' abstract learning rules in an explicit task (Stickgold and Walker, 2013), our implicit learners required sleep to 'uncover' abstract higher-level descriptors of the observed structures and utilize them in subsequent implicit learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with comparison to prior work.

claim: The parallel in behavior between explicit and implicit learning suggests an analogous process for integrating and using new information at different levels of internal representation.
source: This parallel in behavior suggests an analogous process for integrating and using implicitly and explicitly acquired new information at different levels of the existing internal representation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications of the results.

claim: The assignment of participants to different consolidation conditions was not fully randomized due to practical reasons and the online nature of the experiments.
source: A potential shortcoming of the current study is that, for practical reasons and due to the online nature of the experiments, the assignment of participants to the different consolidation conditions was not fully randomized.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The exact timing of participants' acquisition of explicit knowledge is unknown in the current study.
source: A further uncontrolled factor in the current study is the exact timing of participants' acquisition of explicit knowledge. As we only collected the relevant information after the final test phase, we do not know when participants gained explicit knowledge during the experiment.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Assessing explicitness at the end of the study was a deliberate decision to avoid accidentally inducing explicitness.
source: However, assessing explicitness at the end of the study was a deliberate decision as the shortcoming of this method appears less severe than the potential of accidentally inducing explicitness by conducting the exit survey earlier.
evidence: This is a methodological justification provided by the authors.

claim: The danger of inducing explicitness has been amply demonstrated by the results of Experiment 5.
source: This danger of inducing explicitness has been amply demonstrated by the results of Experiment 5.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results of Experiment 5.

claim: Different measures of Statistical Learning can produce diverging results while assessing participants' levels of learning.
source: As a final point, previous studies showed that different measures of Statistical Learning can produce diverging results while assessing participants' levels of learning (Bays et al., 2016; Kiai and Melloni, 2021; Liu et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For implicit participants in Experiment 1, learning in Phase 2 was subject to structure-specific proactive interference in the absence of consolidation.
source: Our results in Experiment 1 suggest that for implicit participants learning in Phase 2 was subject to structure-specific proactive interference in the absence of consolidation as learning of same-structure pairs was hindered by the previous learning of pairs in Phase 1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from Experiment 1.

claim: Quantitative performance in statistical learning improves with explicit instructions.
source: Previous statistical learning experiments reported that quantitative performance improves by explicit instructions (Arciuli et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Performances in the presence and absence of explicit instructions converge over longer exposure.
source: and that performances in the presence and absence of explicit instructions converge over longer exposure (Arató et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results in Experiment 5 are in line with findings showing stronger performance after explicit instructions and convergence between explicit and implicit learning outcomes.
source: Our results in Experiment 5 are in line with those findings by showing a stronger performance after explicit instructions about the task structure and a convergence between the outcomes of explicit and implicit learning.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current results to prior findings.

claim: The study demonstrates the vanishing of differences after sleep consolidation even when the difference between initial implicit and explicit learning results is qualitative rather than just numerical.
source: However, we also go beyond these findings by demonstrating the vanishing of differences after sleep consolidation even in cases when the difference between the initial implicit and explicit learning results prior to consolidation is qualitative rather than just numerically different.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results comparing different consolidation conditions.

claim: The study reports a new repulsion–attraction effect at the level of implicit structure transfer, namely a tradeoff between generalization and interference depending on the presence or absence of sleep-consolidation processes.
source: Second, it reports a new repulsion–attraction effect at the level of implicit structure transfer, namely a tradeoff between generalization and interference depending on the presence or absence of sleep-consolidation processes.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding of the study.

claim: Previously, repulsion–attraction effects have been found either within immediate, implicit, and low-level perceptual processes without linking to sleep, or within high-level categorization setups investigating sleep effects in explicit tasks.
source: Previously, such repulsion–attraction effects have been found either within immediate, implicit, and low-level perceptual processes but without linking the effect to sleep (Daelli et al., 2010; Fritsche et al., 2020; Wei and Stocker, 2015) or within high-level categorization setups that did investigate sleep effects but in the context of explicit tasks (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Djonlagic et al., 2009; Lerner and Gluck, 2019; Lewis and Durrant, 2011; Stickgold and Walker, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The converging sleep-related effects across implicit and explicit contexts might indicate the existence of a more general factorization mechanism in the brain.
source: The converging sleep-related effects across implicit and explicit contexts might indicate the existence of a more general factorization mechanism in the brain that works continuously and at multiple levels during perceptual and cognitive processes following the same computational principles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the broader implications of the results.

claim: In Experiment 1, 251 participants were recruited via prolific.co.
source: In total, 251 participants (92 females, age: mean=28.0, mode=25, SD=9.5) were recruited via prolific.co.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant recruitment.

claim: The study was approved by the Hungarian United Ethical Review Committee for Research in Psychology (EPKEB).
source: The study was approved by the Hungarian United Ethical Review Committee for Research in Psychology (EPKEB), and all participants provided informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: The sample size was chosen to achieve 80% power for expected small effect sizes (d=0.2) in paired t-tests.
source: The sample size was chosen to achieve 80% power for expected small effect sizes (d=0.2) in paired t-tests (needed sample for the implicit subgroup according to power analysis = 198.15) and to account for exclusions.
evidence: This is a methodological justification for the sample size.

claim: Nineteen participants were rejected for failing the attention check criterion.
source: Based on pilot data, we choose 20 seconds combined response time for both attention checks as the cut-off value for inclusion. Nineteen participants were rejected for failing this criterion.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant exclusions.

claim: Three participants were excluded for response bias.
source: Response bias was defined as the proportion with which participants used one of the two response options ('1' and '2'), and participants who were 2.5 SD away from the mean were excluded. Three participants were excluded for failing this criterion.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant exclusions.

claim: After exclusions, 229 participants remained in Experiment 1.
source: This left us with 229 participants after exclusions.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the final sample size.

claim: In Experiment 1, 192 participants were categorized as implicit, 34 as explicit, and 3 were excluded for reporting awareness of the underlying structure.
source: Based on the open responses at the end of the experiment, participants were categorized into one of three groups. Participants who reported no knowledge of pairs were counted as implicit (n=192), participants who reported knowledge of the presence of pairs were counted as explicit (n=34), and participants who also reported the underlying horizontal/vertical structure were excluded from analysis as they were too few for meaningful analysis (n=3).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant categorization.

claim: The stimuli were taken from Fiser and Aslin, 2001 and consisted of 20 abstract black shapes on a white background.
source: The stimuli were taken from Fiser and Aslin, 2001 and consisted of 20 abstract black shapes on a white background (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the stimuli with a citation and reference to Figure 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, 160 scenes were created for the first learning phase and 48 for the second learning phase.
source: In total, 160 scenes were created for the first and 48 for the second learning phase.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the number of scenes.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants passively observed 160 scenes in the first training phase.
source: Participants passively observed 160 scenes in the first training phase.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the procedure.

claim: Each scene was presented for 2 seconds with a 1-second interstimulus interval.
source: Each scene was presented for 2 seconds with a 1-second interstimulus interval (ISI).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about stimulus presentation timing.

claim: In Experiment 1, there was a 2-minute passive break between the two training phases.
source: After a 2-minute passive break, participants passively observed 96 scenes in the second training phase.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the break duration.

claim: Explorative analysis of the trials of the second training phase revealed a strong negative correlation between trials of the novel and the same structure.
source: Explorative analysis of the trials of the second training phase revealed a strong negative correlation between trials of the novel and the same structure (r=−0.432, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a finding from exploratory data analysis.

claim: The negative correlation between novel and same structure trials increases from the first eight trials to the second eight trials.
source: Indeed, for the first eight trials, this correlation is r=−0.209, while it increases to r=−0.435 in the second eight trials.
evidence: This is a finding from exploratory data analysis.

claim: Only the first eight trials were included in all analyses to minimize the consistency effect.
source: Based on this exploration, we included only the first eight trials in all the following analyses to minimize this consistency effect.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on exploratory analysis.

claim: The data was collapsed over vertical and horizontal conditions for all further analysis.
source: The data was collapsed over vertical and horizontal conditions for all further analysis, as a 3 × 2 mixed ANOVA with test type (levels: training 1, same structure, novel structure) as within-subject factor and condition (levels: horizontal, vertical) as between-subject factor showed no significant main effect of condition (F(1, 224)=0.776, p=0.379, BF=0.08, ηp2=0.003) and no significant test type–condition interaction (F(2,448)=0.199, p=0.820, BF=0.04, ηp2=0.001).
evidence: This is a methodological decision justified by statistical analysis.

claim: In Experiment 1, both explicit and implicit learners performed above chance for pairs of the first training phase.
source: Both explicit and implicit learners in Experiment 1 performed above chance for pairs of the first training phase (Expl: M=67.9, SE=4.6, d=0.67, t(33)=3.93, p=0.002, BF = 70.8; Impl: M=55.0, SE=1.1, d=0.32, t(191)=4.46, p<0.001, BF=919).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, the difference between implicit participants' performances with same vs. different higher-order structures was statistically significant.
source: The difference between the implicit participants' performances with same vs. different higher-order structures was statistically significant (Mdiff=8.72, d=0.20, t(191)=2.78, p=0.030, BF=3.38).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: In Experiment 2, explicit learners performed above chance for pairs of the same structure but not pairs of a novel structure in Phase 2.
source: Specifically, explicit learners (n=21) performed above chance for pairs of the same structure (M=66.7, SE=5.8, d=0.63, t(20)=2.87, p=0.038, BF=5.3) but not pairs of a novel structure (M=51.2, SE=5.8, d=0.04, t(20)=0.20, p=0.841, BF=0.23) in the test of Phase 2 pairs.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, there was a 12-hour overnight consolidation phase between Phases 1 and 2.
